new_deep.name: Physical realizability and coordinate validity of a transformer optical microscope
new_deep.goal: I want to determine which established physical system can faithfully represent a trained Vision Transformer's residual dynamics, and where an optical-colloid interpretation breaks mathematically. A fixed image produces 600 token states in 192 dimensions. Each of six pre-normalized blocks alternates attention with a residual MLP update F(x)=sum_c GELU(w_c dot LayerNorm(x)+b_c) v_c+b, with 768 learned pairs of input and output vectors. We visualize each neuron as a reflector whose signed activation weights a push on a colloid; directions and activations are projected into 3D. Training changes the shared weights between checkpoints and is a different clock from propagation through depth. I need established physical counterparts and conditions for realizable optical forces, nonconservative flow, trapping versus transport, and the validity of projected Jacobian rotation or volume measurements. Determine which conclusions require a genuine potential, noise, fluctuation-response calibration, or invariant coordinate choice, and what would falsify the optical interpretation.

new_deep.name: Causal emergence of coordinated neuron force fields during transformer learning
new_deep.goal: I am developing a microscope for how a Vision Transformer learns, tracking the same 600 spatial tokens of fixed images through hundreds of training checkpoints and decomposing each MLP residual update into 768 signed neuron contributions activation times output vector. Preliminary observations include stronger approximate antiparallel output vectors, substantial cancellation among neuron contributions, persistent antisymmetric local Jacobian components, and spatially correlated token motion. I want the closest prior art and a falsifiable publication question about whether training creates coordinated nonconservative transport useful for prediction, rather than changes explained by random high-dimensional geometry, LayerNorm, convolutional overlap or shared weight updates. Find studies of neuron cooperation and cancellation, token-conditioned vector fields and Jacobians during training, and causal ablations linking those quantities to task performance. Separate what has already been established in language models or depth dynamics from what remains open for image tokens across training.

new_deep.name: Identifying stochastic confinement from neural representation trajectories
new_deep.goal: I want to assess whether the trajectory of a fixed image token observed across training checkpoints can legitimately be called a colloid confined in a moving trap. The token is recomputed from shared neural network weights updated with AdamW, batch randomness, weight decay and gradient clipping. Observed trajectories show slow drift, negative successive-increment correlations and a nearly flat long-lag mean-square displacement. An Ornstein-Uhlenbeck fit currently subtracts a centered moving average and late checkpoints are spaced farther apart than the inferred relaxation time. Determine what physical systems with shared stochastic forcing and memory provide a defensible reduced description, how to discriminate genuine restoring response from filtering and omitted variables, and which intervention, response or multiscale tests establish a physical analogy without inferring equilibrium temperature from variance alone.

/Mathematical grounding of an optical tweezer picture of transformer MLP blocks force fields traps and effective temperature (status: completed, created: Oct 12 14:08, updated: Oct 12 14:11)
  Research goal:
  ```
  I visualise one MLP block of a small vision transformer (dimension 192, hidden 768, GELU, pre-LayerNorm, 6 blocks, 600 patch tokens) as an optical system: each hidden neuron c is a fixed "reflector" with an input direction w_c (row of the first linear layer) and an output direction v_c (column of the second linear layer); for token j it emits a beam of brightness z_jc = GELU(w_c · LN(x_j) + b_c) that pushes the token ("colloidal particle") along v_c, so the block update is x_j <- x_j + sum_c z_jc v_c. The same v_c is used for every token (weight sharing), like a telecentric lens that makes all beams of one reflector parallel. During training the weights change (reflectors re-aim). I want the mathematical literature that makes each element of this picture precise and that tells me what is still missing. Specifically: (1) transformers and residual networks as interacting particle systems or neural ODEs where the feed-forward/MLP sublayer is a per-particle convection or force field and attention is the interaction/diffusion term (e.g. operator splitting of multi-particle dynamics), and MLP blocks viewed as key-value memories (input key = first-layer row, output value = second-layer column); (2) when the feed-forward map is a gradient of a potential (conservative force, energy-based transformers, Hopfield-type energies, tied weights) versus non-conservative; Helmholtz/symmetric-antisymmetric decomposition of the Jacobian of a learned vector field and what the symmetric part (stiffness, restoring force, attractor) and antisymmetric part (rotation, circulation) mean for token dynamics; (3) LayerNorm/RMSNorm as projection of tokens onto a hypersphere and its geometric role (the "sphere" in my picture); (4) the physics of optical tweezers and holographic optical trap arrays: trap stiffness, equipartition, power spectral density and corner frequency calibration, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck fluctuations, multiple traps generated by one spatial light modulator, and how these calibration methods could be transferred to estimate stiffness and an effective temperature of token representations; (5) effective temperature of stochastic gradient descent and Adam measured through fluctuation-dissipation relations, and diagnostics of training based on such thermodynamic quantities (temperature, stiffness, entropy production); (6) per-token or per-sample linear response / Jacobian of a layer used as a local trap or stability analysis of representations during training.
  ```
  Summary of results (based on available abstracts and metadata, not full texts):
  ```
  The closest mathematical grounding is a split particle-flow picture: attention couples token states, while the position-wise FFN supplies tokenwise drift, with Transformer layers interpretable as discretized convection–diffusion dynamics [Lu19e]; the FFN’s neurons also act as key–value memory slots [Gev20].
  
  For a pre-LN block, write its token update as \(x^+=x+V\,\phi(W\,\mathrm{LN}(x)+b)+c\). Shared columns of \(V\) give the common output directions in your analogy. In general this vector field is not a gradient: locally, conservativity requires a symmetric Jacobian (on a simply connected domain), a condition not guaranteed by an untied FFN; energy-based formulations impose additional structure [Im15, Zim26]. The local split \(J=(J+J^T)/2+(J-J^T)/2\) separates linearized expansion/contraction from circulation, but is not itself a global potential decomposition [Gar18c].
  
  LayerNorm centers and rescales activations, making a centered sphere a useful idealization; learned affine parameters and numerical epsilon make the exact image more general [Bro23d, Rie24]. Optical-tweezer work supplies transferable estimators—equipartition, OU/PSD corner-frequency fits, and multi-trap calibration [Gie20, Ber04b, Hor08b]—but applying them to token trajectories would be a proposed method, not a physical temperature measurement. SGD fluctuation–dissipation results concern parameter-space dynamics [Yai18, Mig21]; Adam has distinct SDE analyses [Com24b]. Thus a calibrated token-space effective temperature remains unestablished. Per-token Jacobians already support local sensitivity and stability analyses [Aub24, Cow24], offering the most direct route to quantify representation “trap stiffness.”
  ```

  Research goal:
  ```
  I want to know whether anyone has already done the following study, or something close to it, and how novel it is. I train a small vision transformer object detector from scratch (convolutional stem, 600 patch tokens on a 30×20 grid, fixed 2D sine-cosine positional encoding, 6 transformer blocks, a dense per-token head) with AdamW for 60 epochs and save 806 checkpoints. For fixed input images I record the hidden representation of every patch token (the hidden layer of the last MLP block, 768-D, plus a random 128-D projection) at every checkpoint and, in dense runs, at every optimizer step. I then treat the 600 tokens of one image as 600 particles whose "time" is training time (not network depth) and analyse their trajectories with the toolkit of colloidal and glass physics: mean-squared displacement and cage size, non-Gaussian parameter, self-intermediate scattering and stretched-exponential relaxation, aging, four-point susceptibility and dynamic heterogeneity, spatial correlations of mobility, persistence of mobility rankings, pair dispersion, a relative Lindemann ratio over grid neighbours, phonon-like spectra of displacements on the patch grid, Procrustes alignment to remove global rigid motion, and a decomposition of each token's motion into a global component, a slow drift of its vibration centre, and fast vibrations. I compare against a positive control (simulated Brownian colloidal glass) and a negative control (independent Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particles in cooling wells), vary learning rate, data amount, seeds, optimizer (SGD vs AdamW), architecture (CNN control), layer, and dataset. /How individual MLP neuron contributions add up and cancel on a single token in transformers and how this evolves in training (status: completed, created: Oct 14 14:29, updated: Oct 14 14:33)
  Research goal:
  ```
  In a transformer (vision or language), the MLP output for one token is a sum of neuron contributions, each neuron's activation times its output weight vector. I want to find work that studies this sum on a per-token basis: how many neurons contribute substantially, how much their contributions cancel each other (ratio of the norm of the sum to the sum of the norms, destructive interference, opposing neurons, self-repair and erasure), the effective number of contributing neurons (participation ratio, sparsity of activations, dead or dormant neurons), the geometry of the contributing output directions (anisotropy, superposition, polysemantic neurons, rank of the active set), how the output of the MLP block compares in size with the residual stream, and especially how all of these per-token statistics change during training, across layers and between models. Also work that interprets a neuron's output weight vector as a direction it writes into the residual stream (key–value memories, value vectors, logit lens of neurons) and quantifies agreement or disagreement between the input key and the output value of the same neuron. I want to know what is already measured so I can tell which per-token measurements of neuron cooperation would be new, especially for vision transformers and for the course of training.
  ```
  Summary of results (based on available abstracts and metadata, not full texts):
  ```
  Existing work measures token-wise MLP activation sparsity and its evolution during training, but the retrieved literature does not directly quantify how neuron output vectors sum or cancel for a single token; that vector-cooperation measurement—especially in ViTs—appears to be a clear gap [Wil24b, Li22ap].
  
  The closest training-dynamics studies track ReLU activation sparsity, layer-specific patterns, and neuron death [Wil24b], or report sparsity trends across pretraining and model scales [Luo24d, Zha24bj]. These count active or weakly active coordinates, not the effective number of neurons after weighting each activation by its output-vector norm, nor the ratio between the norm of the summed MLP update and the sum of individual contribution norms. Aggregate FFN spectral-rank measures offer adjacent geometry, but not per-token geometry of the active output directions [Jha25e].
  
  For neuron read/write alignment, cosine similarity between input and output weights is directly studied in gated LLMs, with layer-dependent enrichment versus depletion [Ger25b]; key–value memory and vocabulary-space decompositions characterize neuron values and their predictive effects [Gev20, Gev22]. Cancellation and repair work instead emphasizes cross-component or downstream compensation, rather than within-one-token, within-one-MLP vector interference [Rus24b, Mcg23]. Vision work establishes activation sparsity in ViTs [Li22ap] and selective neuron effects in CLIP [Gan24c], but does not supply this cooperation analysis. A focused contribution would track signed/vector-valued neuron contributions, cancellation, effective count, and MLP-update-to-residual scale across checkpoints, layers, and language/vision models.
  ```

/Local force field tensor of a focused beam optical trap and colloid motion through the focus when there is no stable equilibrium (status: completed, created: Oct 15 10:33, updated: Oct 15 10:37)
  Research goal:
  ```
  I compute, exactly and on a 3D grid, the force field felt by one colloid-like particle inside a small cell around it, where the field is produced by hundreds of converging beams (an analogue of a focused-beam optical trap built from many beams). Within the cell the field is almost perfectly linear, F(u) ≈ F0 + J u, so I characterise it by the full 3×3 force-gradient tensor J: its symmetric part (stiffness along three principal axes, which here is usually a saddle: some axes restoring, others repelling, and sometimes repelling in all axes), its trace (divergence: converging or diverging field, like a focusing or defocusing lens), and its antisymmetric part (curl, rotational non-conservative force). The particle is pushed by F0 much farther than the cell size, and the zero of the field almost never lies inside the cell, so the particle is not held at an equilibrium point; it is driven through the focal region. I want the optics and optical-tweezers literature that (1) measures or computes the full stiffness matrix / force-gradient tensor of optical traps, including anisotropy, off-diagonal coupling between axes, and the decomposition of optical forces into gradient (curl-free) and scattering (non-conservative, curl and divergence) parts, including theoretical results on the divergence and curl of optical force fields; (2) maps optical force fields in 3D around the focus experimentally or numerically (force-field reconstruction from Brownian trajectories, scanning a particle through the focus, T-matrix / generalized Lorenz–Mie calculations of force landscapes), including saddle points, off-axis structure, and how aberrations, beam convergence angle and particle size change the field; (3) describes what a particle does in a focused beam when no stable trapping point exists or when the gradient force cannot balance the scattering force: being pushed or guided along the beam axis, passing through the focus, escape trajectories, unstable equilibria, orbiting and spiralling motion in rotational force fields, and stability criteria for trapping; (4) traps formed by multiple intersecting or counter-propagating beams and how the many-beam geometry shapes the local stiffness tensor.
